subsection: 8. The co-operative movement and industrial Belfast: the shipyards

notes.h: Horace Plunkett and the co-operative idea (1889–1894)
notes.b: Plunkett promoted agricultural co-operation as a way to raise farm incomes without political conflict over the land.
points: Horace Plunkett (1854–1932), an Anglo-Irish landowner and Unionist, believed that co-operation among farmers could raise their incomes and improve their productivity.
The first co-operative creamery in Ireland is usually dated to Dromcollogher, Co. Limerick, in 1889 (verify date and location).
Co-operative creameries let small farmers pool their milk, which allowed them to process butter and sell it at better prices than private dealers paid.
Plunkett founded the Irish Agricultural Organisation Society (IAOS) in 1894, to spread co-operative creameries, agricultural credit and farm supply societies.
Credit societies, modelled on continental Raiffeisen banks, lent small sums to farmers, which reduced their dependence on moneylenders and on landlords’ agents.

notes.b: The co-operative movement gained state support through Plunkett’s Recess Committee and the Department of Agriculture, but nationalists and unionists alike were suspicious of it.
points: The Recess Committee of 1895, set up by Plunkett and others, investigated Irish agriculture and recommended a government department to promote farming and technical education.
The Department of Agriculture and Technical Instruction for Ireland was set up in 1899, and Plunkett was its first vice-president.
Nationalists suspected the co-operative movement of being a unionist and landlord device to undermine the Land League tradition and to divert attention from Home Rule.
Unionists were suspicious of the movement’s links to the Irish Parliamentary Party and to the Catholic clergy, and many Protestant farmers in the north stayed out of it.
The movement’s results included a rapid growth of creameries and credit societies by 1914, which supported farming incomes and rural literacy in technical skills.

notes.h: Belfast: the growth of the city and its industries (1860–1914)
notes.b: Belfast grew from a small port into Ireland’s largest industrial city, with linen, engineering and shipbuilding as its main industries.
points: Belfast’s growth in the nineteenth century rested on the linen industry, which drew workers from the surrounding countryside and from the Catholic west to the mills.
Other industries included rope-making, tobacco processing and engineering, and the tobacco factories employed many women alongside the linen mills.
Belfast overtook Dublin in population by the early twentieth century, and it became the largest city in Ireland by the 1900s or 1910s (verify date).
Working conditions in the mills and yards were harsh, with long hours, low pay and little protection against accidents or unemployment.
Belfast’s industrial workers were divided on sectarian lines, and Protestant workers were often given preference in the shipyards and engineering works.

notes.h: Harland and Wolff and the shipyards
notes.b: Harland and Wolff built some of the largest liners of the period, and its success tied Belfast’s economy to the shipping trade.
points: Edward Harland, an Englishman who ran the yard from 1861, and Gustav Wolff, a German-born partner, built the firm into the largest shipbuilder in Belfast.
William Pirrie, a Canadian-born businessman, became a partner in the firm and later its chairman, and he directed its expansion in the early twentieth century.
Workman Clark, founded in 1880 by Frank Workman and George Clark, was the second large shipyard in Belfast and competed with Harland and Wolff for liner orders.
Harland and Wolff built the Olympic-class liners, including the Titanic, which was launched in May 1911 and sank on her maiden voyage in April 1912.
The shipyards employed thousands of men, and the Harland and Wolff yard in particular was one of the largest employers in the city.

notes.h: Sectarian employment and the shipyard expulsions
notes.b: Religious divisions shaped who got work in the shipyards, and the expulsion of Catholic workers in 1886 was the most violent example.
points: In 1886 Protestant workers in the shipyards and engineering works forced Catholic workers out of their jobs, an event that sparked rioting in the city.
Catholic workers were a minority in the shipyards, and their exclusion from skilled work was a recurring feature of Belfast employment.
Protestant unionism linked its economic interest in the shipyards to the defence of the Union, and workers’ fear of Home Rule reinforced sectarian divisions in the yards.

notes.b: Belfast’s industrial economy and its unionist politics contrasted with Dublin’s commercial and political character.
points: Belfast’s economy depended on manufacturing and shipbuilding for export, while Dublin’s economy was based on administration, services and smaller-scale trades.
Belfast’s workforce was more concentrated in large factories and yards, whereas much of Dublin’s workforce was casual and in small workshops.
Belfast was a unionist stronghold with a strong Protestant middle class, while Dublin had a larger nationalist and Catholic majority.
Belfast’s trade unions were often more closely tied to sectarian politics, while Dublin’s labour movement was more influenced by Larkin and Connolly.

notes.b: Judgements compare the co-operative movement’s success in agriculture with the limits of Belfast’s industrial prosperity.
points: Achievement: co-operation spread across Irish agriculture, improving farmers’ incomes, and Belfast became a major industrial centre with world-famous shipbuilding.
Limit: co-operation remained largely outside the north-east, and Belfast’s prosperity was bound up with sectarian division in employment and politics.
Contemporaries split over the co-operative movement: unionists and landlords saw it as beneficial, while many nationalists saw it as a conservative remedy that avoided the land question.
Historians see Belfast’s shipyards as both a symbol of industrial success and an example of how economic interests fed unionist politics.
